unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 8: Advertising and Persuasion! Every day, you are surrounded by messages designed to grab your attention, change your mind, or convince you to buy something. From billboards towering over busy Mogadishu streets to sponsored posts sliding through your social media feed, advertising is everywhere. But how does it work? What techniques do advertisers use to persuade people? And how can you, as a critical thinker, tell the difference between honest information and clever manipulation?
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and the four vocabulary groups. Read and annotate The Power of Persuasion, the interview with Zara and the story Code Name: Bonanza. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability across the three texts. Apply the eight grammar focuses in the merged practice workshops. Draft and revise a persuasive advertisement, review or essay. Present, debate, reflect and complete the quiz.

visual.alt: Learners analysing advertising, persuasion and audience effect

readings.title: The Power of Persuasion
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Walk down any busy street in Mogadishu, Nairobi, or Addis Ababa and you will be surrounded by advertising. Posters shout about products on sale. Shop windows display items in stock. Radio jingles repeat catchy slogans. Sponsored posts fill your phone screen. Advertising is so pervasive that most people barely notice it anymore — yet its influence on our choices is enormous. Understanding how persuasion works is one of the most lucrative skills a young person can develop, not to make money from selling, but to protect yourself from being sold to without your knowledge.
Although advertising has existed for centuries, modern techniques are far more intricate than a simple market trader calling out prices. Today, advertisers use psychology, data analysis, and visual design to target specific audiences. A well-branded product does not just describe what it does — it creates a feeling. A sports drink advert does not simply say "this drink contains vitamins." Instead, it shows athletes running through rain, their muscles glistening, while dramatic music plays. The message is not about vitamins — it is about strength, ambition, and belonging to a winning team. The drink is dubbed a "performance booster" and sold at a premium.
One of the most powerful advertising techniques is the use of emotional appeal. Advertisers know that people make decisions based on feelings first and logic second. A charity advertisement might show a desolate landscape and a child with a sad expression to make viewers feel sympathy. A perfume advertisement might use soft lighting, elegant models, and a dainty bottle to create feelings of luxury and desire. Created by teams of designers and psychologists, these advertisements are carefully crafted to bypass your rational mind and speak directly to your emotions.
Whereas emotional appeals target the heart, logical appeals target the mind. These advertisements use facts, statistics, and comparisons. You might see claims like "9 out of 10 dentists recommend this toothpaste" or "our battery lasts 50% longer than the competition." The more specific the data, the more trustworthy the advert appears. However, an attentive reader will ask: where did these numbers come from? Were the statistics collected fairly? A cunning advertiser can present true facts in misleading ways — if consumers were more critical, fewer false claims would succeed.
Another technique is social proof — the idea that if other people are doing something, it must be good. Reviews, testimonials, and celebrity endorsements all work on this principle. When a fast-selling product displays thousands of five-star reviews, shoppers feel reassured. When a famous footballer wears a particular brand of trainers, fans want the same pair. Advertisers understand that momentum is powerful: the more people buy a product, the more others want it too. This creates a cycle that can turn an ordinary product into a bonanza of sales.
Not all advertising is harmful. Public health campaigns use persuasive techniques to encourage good habits: washing hands, getting vaccinated, staying in school. Environmental organisations use emotional appeals to protect forests and oceans. While commercial advertising aims to sell products, social advertising aims to change behaviour for the better. The key difference is purpose: is the message designed to help you, or is it designed to help the company's bank balance?
In East Africa, advertising is evolving rapidly. Mobile phone companies run some of the most visible campaigns, offering data bundles on sale and airtime at a discount. Small businesses use social media to reach customers they could never have found before. A tailor in Hargeisa can now advertise her bountiful collection of fabrics to customers across the region. Although this creates enormous opportunity, it also means that young people are exposed to more persuasive messages than any previous generation. Learning to analyse these messages — to question who made them, why, and what they want you to do — is no longer optional. It is essential.
Here is the scale of what you are up against. The global advertising industry spends over 700 billion US dollars every year — more than the entire GDP of many countries. The average person sees between 4,000 and 10,000 advertisements every single day once online adverts, product labels and brand logos are counted. Even the word "propaganda" originally just meant "spreading information"; it only gained its negative meaning after it was used for political manipulation in the twentieth century. The messages will keep coming. The question is whether you will read them, or merely receive them.

readings.title: Adverts Everywhere: An Interview about Advertising Ethics
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Interviewer: What do you think about advertising in East Africa today?
Zara: Honestly, it is everywhere. Every time I open my phone, I see adverts for data bundles on sale, new clothes and food delivery apps. It is hard to escape.
Interviewer: Do you think these adverts influence your choices?
Zara: They do, even when I try to resist. Although I know that many adverts exaggerate, I still find myself wanting things I see online. The well-branded products look so appealing.
Interviewer: Can you give an example?
Zara: Last month, I saw an advert for a fast-selling pair of trainers. The advert said they were "the most comfortable shoes ever made." Created by a famous designer, the trainers looked amazing. I convinced myself that I needed them. But when I bought them, they were not as comfortable as the advert claimed. I felt apprehensive about wasting my money.
Interviewer: What did you learn from that experience?
Zara: I learned to be more attentive when I see adverts. Now I always check reviews myself before buying anything. My mother said that if she were my age, she would have the same problem, because advertising is much more intricate now than it used to be. The more I learn about persuasion techniques, the less likely I am to be tricked.
Interviewer: Some people say that strong branding is simply good business. Where do you draw the line between persuasion and manipulation?
Zara: Persuasion gives you true information in an appealing way, but manipulation hides or twists the facts. If an advert must hide the truth to work, then it has crossed the line. A company can be proud of its product and still tell the truth about it.
Interviewer: What about reviews and influencers? Do you trust them?
Zara: I am careful. Some reviews are written by real customers, but others are paid for and never say so. When an influencer praises a product with huge gusto but hides the payment, that is social proof being manufactured, not earned. I look for balanced reviews that mention at least one weakness.
Interviewer: Should governments create stricter rules for advertising on social media?
Zara: It is a difficult balance. Misleading adverts should be banned, because young people are especially vulnerable, and experts have said that social media advertising is more precisely targeted than anything that came before it. At the same time, strict regulation would impede the small businesses that rely on social media to reach their first customers. A tailor with a bountiful collection of fabrics can now find buyers across the whole region without paying for a single billboard. I would punish dishonesty severely and leave honest sellers alone.
Interviewer: Do you think traditional advertising is finished?
Zara: People keep calling billboards and radio jingles obsolete, but I am not convinced. A poster on a busy road reaches everyone, not just the people an algorithm selects. What is truly becoming obsolete is the lazy advert that assumes nobody will check its claims. The audience has changed, and an indifferent shrug is now the most dangerous response a brand can earn.
Interviewer: What advice would you give to other young people?
Zara: Do not believe everything you see. The more colourful and exciting an advert looks, the more carefully you should examine it. Teach yourself to ask two questions: who made this advert, and what do they want me to do? If every young person asked those questions, misleading advertising would diminish quickly.
Interviewer: That sounds like advice worth printing on a poster.
Zara: Maybe, though I would read the small print on that poster too.

readings.title: Code Name: Bonanza, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The morning air in Mogadishu was pungent with the smell of roasted coffee and car fumes as the courtyard of the technology academy buzzed with students. Posters flapped against walls, advertising the annual "Innovation for Impact" challenge. The national competition brought together top student teams to pitch projects that combined technology with social good.
This year's theme: sustainable urban living.
Imani eyed the poster as she passed, already knowing every detail. She had emerged as one of the most promising coders in school, known for her quiet focus and sharp aptitude in algorithms. But she was not competing alone.
"We have got five days," said Rohan, her teammate. He had a bold demeanor and the annoying habit of tapping pens when thinking. "We can still win if we push."
"If we had more time," Imani muttered, "we would perfect the drone's navigation."
Their project, a waste-sorting drone, was promising but glitchy. Sometimes it confused recyclable plastic for food waste. It was clever — maybe too clever — and the mechanics were intricate.
The school's tech lab, usually quiet, had turned into a battlefield. Tools and tablets were everywhere. Tension built with each hour.
Their biggest adversary was Team Horizon, led by Nadir — the kind of competitor who smiled sweetly while planting doubts in your mind.
"Nice drone," he said one afternoon, passing Imani's table. "Shame it is not... reliable."
Imani raised an eyebrow. "Our testing has just begun."
Nadir grinned. "So has ours. We have dubbed it 'The Beacon.'"
The name had already shown up on flyers around the campus. Well-branded. Fast-selling. Future-ready.
Created by a cunning team, The Beacon seemed flawless. Too flawless. Rumours swirled that Team Horizon had copied elements from online builds.
When Imani told Rohan, he looked apprehensive.
"If they cheated, should we report it?"
Imani shook her head. "Only if we have proof. Otherwise, it is just... noise."
On Wednesday, all teams gave a short demo. When it was Team Spark's turn, Rohan stepped up, voice steady.
"Our drone sorts waste mid-air using object recognition. It runs on solar power and can recharge at smart stations."
The drone rose. For a moment, all was smooth.
Then it wobbled, bumped into a shelf, and dropped a piece of cardboard meant to be sorted.
A few students laughed.
Imani clenched her fists, blaming herself.
The judges nodded politely, saying little. Their eyes moved to Team Horizon, whose prototype hovered like a dream, sorting items into labelled bins with almost robotic grace.
Applause followed. One judge even whispered, "Now that is a bonanza of an idea."
Imani felt the momentum diminish. Their odds shrank like morning mist.
Later that evening, Rohan slammed a tablet down. "It is not fair. He is using tech we cannot trace. I bet it is not even original."
Imani nodded, thinking. "Then let us beat them differently."
"How?"
"The more belligerent we get, the less people listen. But the more we refine, the more we show who we are."
The team worked with new gusto, rewriting the sorting code and simplifying the drone's shell to improve balance. Imani even wrote a script in the passive voice for the final pitch:
"The drone is launched by solar timing. Waste is identified by AI and sorted automatically. Maintenance is managed remotely."
She trained herself to speak with calm authority. Rohan changed his tone from fiery to firm. The more they rehearsed, the more natural the answers became, and they practised until the pitch felt smooth.

readings.title: Code Name: Bonanza, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Final day.
Bright lights filled the auditorium. Parents, local reporters, and school heads sat in rows. Each team had ten minutes.
Team Horizon went first. Nadir's tone was slick, his smile wide.
"Our product, The Beacon, will transform waste into wealth."
He walked through their process, but avoided technical questions. One judge asked about the source code.
"Proprietary," Nadir replied. "Protected for future commercial use."
Imani caught a flash of confusion among the judges.
Then it was Team Spark's turn.
Created through weeks of testing, their new version was lighter, steadier, and clear in function.
Imani spoke: "Built for local streets, the drone adapts to changes in light and wind. It was designed with community spaces in mind."
Their presentation included video clips, one where the drone dropped waste neatly into bins outside a park. The judges murmured approval.
Afterward, during the question-and-answer session, a judge asked, "How did you overcome your early bugs?"
"We evaluated each failure," Imani answered. "And improved based on them. We learned from ourselves."
There was a long pause. Then applause.
Later, as everyone waited for results, Nadir approached.
"That was... solid," he said.
Imani nodded, cautious.
"You are calm," he added. "I would be panicking if I were you."
"We did our best," she said, refusing to be drawn into his insolent games.
He stepped closer. "I could offer a concession. Maybe we say we collaborate next year. Share ideas."
Rohan narrowed his eyes. "We are not interested."
"Fine." Nadir walked away, his demeanor suddenly tense.
Moments later, the announcements began.
In third place: a drone that composted banana peels.
In second: The Beacon.
The hall gasped.
First place: Team Spark.
A roar followed. Imani barely heard anything beyond the sound of Rohan yelling in joy and hugging her.
The judges explained: "Team Spark impressed not only with innovation but with transparency and teamwork. They demonstrated growth, strategy, and an eye for ethical application."
Back at the lab, a breeze entered through the open windows. Plans and sketches billowed off desks. Imani caught one.
"Looks like we need a filing system," she said, laughing.
The room felt capacious, suddenly full of promise. Empty space had become opportunity.
Rohan was already scribbling ideas. "Maybe we create a multi-use drone next — well-branded and bright."
Imani smiled. "We will need to study more. Better sensors. Better balance."
"If we had the funding," Rohan mused, "we would launch a full pilot in the summer."
"If we had the funding," Imani echoed, "we would create jobs too."
Outside, clouds undulated in waves across the sky. The competition was over, but momentum was building.
Imani looked at her hands. They smelled faintly of soldering metal and soap. She had fought an uphill battle — not with belligerence, but with reason.
And that, she thought, was how to win with integrity.

comprehension.question: Zara advises that the more colourful and exciting an advert looks, the more carefully you should examine it. Explain what she means and how her trainers experience supports this advice.

comprehension.question: The story ends with Imani thinking that this "was how to win with integrity." Using events from part 2, explain how Team Spark's victory proves the story's moral.
comprehension.correctAnswer: In part 2 Nadir avoided technical questions and called The Beacon proprietary, while Imani answered honestly about the early bugs, saying the team evaluated each failure and learned from ourselves, so the judges rewarded transparency and teamwork over slick branding.
comprehension.explanation: A synthesis question drawing together transparency, the proprietary refusal and the moral of the ending.

grammar.title: Prepositions Preceding Nouns
grammar.explanation: Prepositions are small words that show the relationship between a noun and the rest of the sentence. In advertising language they sit directly before nouns to build fixed phrases such as on sale, in stock and at a discount, and learning each phrase as one complete unit makes your English sound natural and precise.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Choose the preposition the phrase demands, place it before the noun, then use the whole phrase in a sentence.
on sale — The shoes are on sale this week. | in stock — The toy is in stock at all our stores. | for a limited time — This offer is valid for a limited time. | at a discount — You can buy it at a discount today. | on display — The new collection is on display in the window. | in demand — These phones are in high demand. | for commercial use — The software is for commercial use only. | with interest — You can pay later with interest.
Many of these phrases are fixed: English says on sale, never in sale. The same noun can also change meaning with a different preposition — in time means not late, while on time means at the exact planned moment.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing the item is in sale this week; the fixed phrase takes on, so the correct sentence is the item is on sale this week. Leaving the preposition out entirely, as in the book is table, breaks the sentence — it needs on the table.
grammar.memoryTip: Prepositions are position words: they position a noun in relation to everything around it, so learn each advertising phrase as one welded unit.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill each blank with on, in, for or at: 1) The special offer is ______ sale until Friday. 2) These headphones are ______ stock in all colours. 3) This discount is available ______ a limited time. 4) You can buy the jacket ______ a reduced price today. 5) The new phones are ______ high demand this month.
Part B — complete with the right preposition: 1) The laptop comes ______ a two-year guarantee. 2) All items are ______ display in the shop window. 3) The advertisement was made ______ commercial use.
Part C — write three sentences advertising something from your school fair, each using a different phrase from the list.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) on (on sale) 2) in (in stock) 3) for (for a limited time) 4) at (at a reduced price) 5) in (in high demand).
Part B: 1) with (with a two-year guarantee) 2) on (on display) 3) for (for commercial use).
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): self-check that each of your three sentences places one full fixed phrase from the list (on sale, in stock, for a limited time, at a discount, on display, in demand, for commercial use, with interest) directly before its noun, exactly as in the rule's examples. Model sentences to compare against: "The school jumpers are on sale this week." / "Fresh samosas are in stock at the food stall." / "Tickets are available for a limited time only."

grammar.title: Passive Voice (Present and Past)
grammar.explanation: The passive voice turns the spotlight onto the action or its receiver instead of the doer, which is why advertisers love it: the product is sold, the aisles are cleaned, and the company itself quietly disappears from the sentence. It is equally common in news reports, scientific writing and formal descriptions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present passive: subject + is or are + past participle — The product is sold in fifty countries. The aisles are cleaned every morning.
Past passive: subject + was or were + past participle — The product was dubbed a bonanza by the press. The cake was eaten by the children.
The agent is optional: add by + doer when it matters (The meal was cooked by the chef) and leave it out when it does not (The homework is completed every evening).
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping the form of to be, as in the book read by the students — the passive always needs it: the book is read by the students. Swapping subject and object produces nonsense such as the chef was cooked by the meal.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of the passive as a flipped sentence: the receiver moves to the front, then comes a form of to be, then the past participle, with by + doer only when the doer matters.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite in the passive voice: 1) The choir sings the song every week. 2) The students finished the homework yesterday. 3) The artist painted the picture last year. 4) The company designs the adverts. 5) The teacher read the story to the class.
Part B — rewrite these advertising sentences in the passive: 1) The company launched the new product last month. 2) The school organises the innovation challenge every year. 3) The team tested the drone in three different locations. 4) The judges awarded first place to Team Spark.
Part C — write two passive sentences describing how a product you own was made and sold.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) The song is sung by the choir every week. 2) The homework was finished by the students yesterday. 3) The picture was painted by the artist last year. 4) The adverts are designed by the company. 5) The story was read to the class by the teacher.
Part B: 1) The new product was launched by the company last month. 2) The innovation challenge is organised by the school every year. 3) The drone was tested by the team in three different locations. 4) First place was awarded to Team Spark by the judges (also acceptable: Team Spark was awarded first place by the judges).
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): self-check that each sentence uses subject + a form of to be (is/are/was/were) + past participle, adding by + the maker only if it matters. Model example to compare your work against: "This bag was made in a small workshop and was sold at the market."

grammar.title: Clauses Beginning with Past Participles
grammar.explanation: A past participle clause opens a sentence with a verb form ending in -ed, -en, -t or -n, packing extra information into a few words before the main clause arrives — the signature move of product descriptions and advertising copy.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Choose a past participle, add its detail, then a comma, then the main clause: Created by a cunning team, the ad drew attention.
More examples: Excited by the surprise party, she smiled widely. Written in a hurry, the note was difficult to read. Built by skilled workers, the bridge is strong and beautiful. Designed for outdoor use, the speaker is waterproof.
Always check the subject: the person or thing described by the participle must be the subject of the main clause.
grammar.commonMistake: Forgetting the comma, as in Created by a cunning team the ad drew attention — the clause must be sealed off before the main clause. Watch for dangling subjects too: Designed for outdoor use, the shop sold the speaker wrongly suggests the shop was designed for outdoor use.
grammar.memoryTip: A participle clause is a snapshot taken just before the main event: it sets the scene in a few words, then the comma opens the curtain.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the correct past participle: 1) ______ (excite) by the performance, the audience cheered loudly. 2) ______ (prepare) for the test, she studied all night. 3) ______ (design) by local engineers, the bridge won an award. 4) ______ (shock) by the news, they sat in silence.
Part B — now these: 1) ______ (build) for rough conditions, the phone can survive drops and water. 2) ______ (inspire) by the competition, the students worked harder than ever. 3) ______ (write) in plain language, the instructions were easy to follow. 4) ______ (create) by local artists, the murals attracted tourists from across the region.
Part C — rewrite two sentences from The Power of Persuasion so that each begins with a past participle clause.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) Excited by the performance, the audience cheered loudly. 2) Prepared for the test, she studied all night. 3) Designed by local engineers, the bridge won an award. 4) Shocked by the news, they sat in silence.
Part B: 1) Built for rough conditions, the phone can survive drops and water. 2) Inspired by the competition, the students worked harder than ever. 3) Written in plain language, the instructions were easy to follow. 4) Created by local artists, the murals attracted tourists from across the region.
Part C: this part asks you to rewrite two of your own chosen sentences from the reading 'The Power of Persuasion,' so there is no single fixed answer — use this self-check method instead. Pick a sentence from that passage containing a passive verb or an -ed/-en form, move that participle (with its own detail) to the front, add a comma, then let the rest of the original sentence become the main clause, keeping the same subject on both sides of the comma. Two worked models using real sentences from the passage: original "The drink is dubbed a 'performance booster' and sold at a premium" becomes "Dubbed a 'performance booster', the drink is sold at a premium." Original "it only gained its negative meaning after it was used for political manipulation in the twentieth century" becomes "Used for political manipulation in the twentieth century, the word gained its negative meaning." Check your own two rewrites against this same pattern, and watch for a dangling subject as flagged in the common mistake above.

grammar.title: Reflexive Pronouns
grammar.explanation: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and appear when the subject and object of a sentence are the same person, or when you want to stress that someone acted alone — which is exactly why adverts urge you to treat yourself.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I becomes myself | you becomes yourself | he becomes himself | she becomes herself | it becomes itself | we becomes ourselves | you (plural) becomes yourselves | they becomes themselves.
Examples: She taught herself to speak with calm authority. We prepared the presentation ourselves. He bought the gift for himself. In the unit story, Team Spark tell the judges: We learned from ourselves.
grammar.commonMistake: Inserting a reflexive where the subject and object are different people: I saw myself the teacher is wrong because you saw someone else — simply write I saw the teacher.
grammar.memoryTip: A reflexive pronoun is a boomerang: however far the sentence throws it, it always curves back to the subject.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill each blank with the correct reflexive pronoun: 1) I can design the poster by ______. 2) She convinced ______ that the product was worth buying. 3) They built the drone all by ______. 4) You should believe in ______. 5) He prepared the advertising pitch by ______.
Part B — now these: 1) I taught ______ how to edit videos by watching tutorials online. 2) We tested the product ______ before recommending it to others. 3) They convinced ______ that the investment was worthwhile.
Part C — write two sentences about something you taught yourself to do, each using a different reflexive pronoun.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) I can design the poster by myself. 2) She convinced herself that the product was worth buying. 3) They built the drone all by themselves. 4) You should believe in yourself. 5) He prepared the advertising pitch by himself.
Part B: 1) I taught myself how to edit videos by watching tutorials online. 2) We tested the product ourselves before recommending it to others. 3) They convinced themselves that the investment was worthwhile.
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): self-check that each sentence's reflexive pronoun matches its own subject (I/myself, she/herself, they/themselves, and so on) and that the subject and object genuinely refer to the same person. Model example to compare your work against: "I taught myself how to bake bread last year." / "She pushed herself to finish the race."

grammar.title: Second Conditional
grammar.explanation: The second conditional imagines situations that are not real right now — dreams, wishes and speculation — and advertisers exploit it to let customers picture life with the product already in their hands: if you had this phone, you would never miss a moment.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Structure: If + past simple, subject + would + base verb.
If I had the aptitude, I would launch a lucrative brand. If we had more time, we would perfect the drone's navigation. If they had bigger budgets, they would film in three cities.
In the if-clause, formal English uses were for every subject: If I were you, I would compare prices first.
grammar.commonMistake: Using was in the if-clause, as in If I was a bird, instead of the special form were, or letting the present tense sneak in: If I have a million dollars, I would travel needs the past form had.
grammar.memoryTip: Call it the dream structure: the past tense signals that you are dreaming, and would signals what happens inside the dream — If I had pairs with I would.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete with the second conditional: 1) If I ______ (be) the president, I ______ (make) education free. 2) If my friend ______ (have) a car, we ______ (go) on a road trip. 3) If she ______ (know) the answer, she ______ (tell) us. 4) If we ______ (have) the funding, we ______ (launch) a pilot programme. 5) If he ______ (be) an advertiser, he ______ (create) only honest adverts.
Part B — finish these advertising ideas in your own words: 1) If this offer were genuine, ... 2) If customers compared prices more carefully, ... 3) If I designed the campaign, ...
Part C — write one second conditional sentence that a charity could use in a fundraising advert.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) If I were the president, I would make education free. 2) If my friend had a car, we would go on a road trip. 3) If she knew the answer, she would tell us. 4) If we had the funding, we would launch a pilot programme. 5) If he were an advertiser, he would create only honest adverts.
Part B (open-ended completions — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): self-check that each completion keeps the would + base verb pattern in the result. Model completions to compare against: 1) "If this offer were genuine, it would not disappear the moment I tried to redeem it." 2) "If customers compared prices more carefully, they would notice that many 'discounts' are not real savings." 3) "If I designed the campaign, I would use honest statistics instead of vague claims."
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): self-check that your sentence follows If + past simple, subject + would + base verb. Model example to compare your work against: "If more people donated even a small amount each month, thousands of children would gain access to education."

grammar.title: Comparatives, Compound Adjectives and Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: This workshop gathers the unit's three remaining tools for analysing adverts: the more / the less comparatives describe cause and effect, hyphenated compound adjectives compress a sales pitch into a single word, and reported speech lets you relay an advertiser's claims without quoting them directly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparatives of cause and effect follow the pattern the more or the less + clause, twice: The more you practise, the better you get. The more belligerent the tone, the less effective the message. The less sugar you eat, the healthier you feel.
Compound adjectives take a hyphen before a noun: well-branded products, a fast-selling toy, a multi-use tool, long-lasting batteries, high-quality fabric, eco-friendly packaging — but after the noun the hyphen disappears: the products are well branded.
Reported speech shifts the tense back one step, changes the pronouns and drops the quotation marks: The manager said, "The offer is a concession" becomes The manager said that the offer was a concession. She claimed, "It is obsolete" becomes She claimed that it was obsolete. Questions use if, whether or the question word: He asked whether I was buying it; she asked why it was on sale.
grammar.commonMistake: Each tool has its own trap: dropping the twin the (More you study, better you get), losing the hyphen (the multi use tool), and forgetting the tense shift (She said that she speaks three languages should be She said that she spoke three languages).
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a seesaw for the comparatives, a hyphen as the handshake joining two describing words, and a time machine for reported speech — present travels back to past, will to would, can to could.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete the comparatives: 1) The ______ you read, the ______ you learn. 2) The ______ creative the advert, the ______ people remember it. 3) The ______ noise there is, the ______ we can hear each other. 4) The ______ honest the message, the ______ consumers trust the brand. 5) The ______ aggressive the salesperson, the ______ comfortable the customer feels.
Part B — fill each gap with the best compound adjective from this set: well-branded, fast-selling, multi-use, eco-friendly, long-lasting. 1) This new gadget is a ______ tool for cooking, cleaning and repairs. 2) The ______ shoes are the latest trend among young people. 3) The ______ toy is flying off the shelves in every store. 4) Our ______ packaging is made from recycled materials. 5) This ______ battery will power your device for two whole days.
Part C — change into reported speech: 1) The teacher said, "You must complete your homework." 2) My friend said, "I will join you later." 3) Dad said, "This movie is great!" 4) The advertiser claimed, "Our product is the best on sale." 5) She asked, "Why is this so expensive?"

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) The more you read, the more you learn. 2) The more creative the advert, the more people remember it. 3) The more noise there is, the less we can hear each other. 4) The more honest the message, the more consumers trust the brand. 5) The more aggressive the salesperson, the less comfortable the customer feels. (Each blank pair should stay logically consistent with cause and effect, as in the rule's own examples — 'more' paired with 'more' when the two things increase together, 'more' paired with 'less' when one rises as the other falls.)
Part B: 1) multi-use 2) well-branded 3) fast-selling 4) eco-friendly 5) long-lasting.
Part C: 1) The teacher said that we/they must complete our/their homework ("must" may also become "had to"). 2) My friend said that she/he would join us/me later. 3) Dad said that the movie was great. 4) The advertiser claimed that their product was the best on sale. 5) She asked why that was so expensive.

writing.title: Writing 1: Persuasive Advertisement
writing.promptAndInstructions: You have been hired to advertise a brand-new product of your own invention: a gadget, a food product, a piece of clothing or a service. Write a full-page advertisement of 250 to 300 words that includes a catchy name and slogan using a compound adjective, an emotional appeal with vivid description, a logical appeal with at least one statistic, social proof built on a comparative such as the more people discover it, the more they love it, a call to action using a prepositional phrase such as available on sale for a limited time, and at least one passive voice sentence.
writing.modelText: Introducing the AquaPure Water Bottle — the well-branded, fast-selling hydration solution that everyone is talking about. Designed by award-winning engineers, the AquaPure keeps your water cold for twenty-four hours. Nine out of ten testers said they would never switch back. The more people discover it, the more they love it. Treat yourself today: the AquaPure is on sale for a limited time.
writing.expectedLength: Five short paragraphs of advertisement copy
writing.successCriteria: I created a memorable name and slogan; used one compound adjective, one comparative, one passive sentence and one prepositional phrase; balanced emotional and logical appeals; ended with a clear call to action; checked spelling and punctuation
writing.support: Plan the six required ingredients as a checklist before drafting, and study the advert examples in The Power of Persuasion.
writing.extension: Write a second, honest version of the same advert and annotate which persuasive choices you toned down and why.

writing.title: Writing 2: Critical Product Review
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose a product you own or have used — a phone, a bag, a pair of shoes, a food item — and write a review of 250 to 300 words that analyses it honestly. Introduce the product and how you got it, use reported speech to describe what the advertising promised, describe your actual experience with a reflexive pronoun such as I tested it myself, weigh strengths against weaknesses with contrast language, and close with a recommendation built on a conditional sentence.
writing.modelText: The company claimed that the headphones were the most comfortable ever made, so I tested them myself for three weeks. Although the sound quality impressed me, the cushioning flattened within days. If I had known about that weakness, I would have chosen a different pair.
writing.successCriteria: I described the product and its advertising claims accurately; used reported speech and a reflexive pronoun; balanced strengths and weaknesses fairly; finished with a justified recommendation; revised for accuracy
writing.support: List the advert's promises in one column and your real experience in another before you draft.
writing.extension: Compare your product against a rival and evaluate which company's advertising is more trustworthy, citing one piece of evidence for each.

writing.title: Writing 3: How Advertising Shapes Our Choices
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an analytical essay of 250 to 300 words about how advertising influences the choices young people make. Explain what advertising is and why understanding it matters, analyse one technique — emotional appeal, logical appeal or social proof — with an example, discuss whether advertising is always honest using vocabulary such as cunning, elusive and attentive, and conclude with your own advice built on a comparative: the more we understand persuasion, the better our choices become.
writing.modelText: Advertising surrounds young people from the moment they wake, and its techniques deserve close attention. Social proof is perhaps the most powerful: when thousands of five-star reviews appear beside a fast-selling product, shoppers feel reassured before they have examined a single fact. Yet an attentive reader soon notices that some praise is manufactured. The more we understand persuasion, the better our choices become.
writing.successCriteria: I defined advertising and its purpose; analysed one technique with a concrete example; evaluated honesty using precise unit vocabulary; concluded with reasoned advice; used cohesive devices between paragraphs
writing.support: Reread the social proof and emotional appeal paragraphs in The Power of Persuasion and note one quotation to discuss.
writing.extension: Add a paragraph on social advertising for good causes and weigh whether the same techniques become acceptable when the purpose changes.

writing.title: Writing 4: Newspaper Report on the Challenge
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short newspaper article of five to eight sentences reporting Team Spark's victory in the Innovation for Impact challenge. Give the article a headline, report the key events in order, and use reported speech to quote at least two people from the story — for example, the judges' explanation and one of the finalists.
writing.modelText: STUDENT DRONE TAKES TOP PRIZE. Team Spark won the national Innovation for Impact challenge yesterday with a waste-sorting drone rebuilt after a failed demonstration. The judges said that the team had impressed them with transparency and teamwork. Imani told reporters that the team had evaluated each failure and improved because of it.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote an informative headline; reported events in a logical order; converted at least two quotations into accurate reported speech; kept a formal news register; checked every tense shift
writing.support: Underline the judges' and finalists' spoken lines in the story before converting them into reported speech.
writing.extension: Add a final paragraph reporting Nadir's reaction, keeping the tone factual rather than mocking.

writing.title: Writing 5: Imani's Diary Entry
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are Imani on the night after the final. Write her diary entry of six to eight sentences about the day, using at least three unit vocabulary words, one passive voice sentence and one reflexive pronoun. Let her honest feelings show: the apprehension before the pitch, the moment the results were announced, and what she plans to do next.
writing.modelText: I was apprehensive all morning, yet the pitch was delivered exactly as we rehearsed it. When our name was announced, the hall seemed to tilt. I keep reminding myself that we won through evidence, not noise. Tomorrow the real work begins.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in a believable first-person voice; included three unit words, one passive sentence and one reflexive pronoun; showed feelings changing across the day; ended looking forward
writing.support: List the day's events from the story in order first, then choose the three moments that mattered most to Imani.
writing.extension: Write a second entry dated five years later, reflecting on what the competition taught her about integrity.

writing.title: Writing 6: The Rival's Concession
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a paragraph of five to six sentences from Nadir's perspective, explaining why he offered Imani a concession after the presentations and how he felt when Rohan rejected it. Use at least two unit vocabulary words and one second conditional sentence. Then add a short closing paragraph in your own voice explaining what the story's moral — the more cunning the path, the less lasting the reward — means to you.
writing.modelText: I offered them a concession because the momentum had clearly shifted and an alliance would protect The Beacon's name. If I had built the drone honestly, I would not have feared the judges' questions. Watching them refuse me, I understood that a slick pitch cannot replace real work.
writing.expectedLength: One developed paragraph plus a closing reflection paragraph
writing.successCriteria: I wrote convincingly from the rival's viewpoint; used two unit words and one second conditional; explained both the offer and the rejection; connected the moral to my own experience
writing.support: Reread Nadir's lines in part 2 and note what his sudden change of demeanor reveals about his motives.
writing.extension: Rewrite the paragraph as Nadir's apology message to Team Spark, keeping his pride visible between the lines.

activities.title: Activities 1: Advert Analysis
activities.instructionsAndItems: Find a real advertisement — from a newspaper, a website, a poster or a screenshot from social media. Stick it in your notebook or describe it in detail, then answer: What product or service is being advertised? Who is the target audience — children, teenagers, adults or parents? Which persuasive techniques does it use: emotional appeal, logical appeal, social proof or celebrity endorsement? Does it use prepositional phrases such as on sale, in stock or for a limited time? Does it use compound adjectives such as well-branded or fast-selling? Is the advert honest, or do any claims seem exaggerated? Finally, rate its effectiveness out of ten and justify your rating.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 2: Before and After
activities.instructionsAndItems: Many products that were once lucrative have become obsolete. Choose three technologies that are no longer widely used — for example cassette tapes, fax machines or film cameras. For each one, write three sentences: a passive voice sentence explaining what it was and why it was popular, such as cassette tapes were used by millions of people to listen to music; a comparative sentence explaining why it faded, such as the more digital music improved, the less people needed cassettes; and a second conditional sentence imagining its return, such as if cassette tapes were reintroduced today, young people would find them charming but impractical.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 3: Create a Brand Identity
activities.instructionsAndItems: Imagine you are starting a small business in your local area — a bakery, a tutoring service, a clothing shop or a tech repair studio. Create a complete brand identity: a business name that uses a compound adjective, such as Quick-Fix Tech Repairs; a short, memorable slogan; a written description of the logo in three to four sentences; a note on your target audience and why they need you; and an advertising paragraph of five to six sentences using at least three unit vocabulary words, one passive voice sentence and one prepositional phrase.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 4: Vocabulary Crossword Clues
activities.instructionsAndItems: Write crossword-style clues for ten unit vocabulary words. Each clue should be a definition or a sentence with a blank, plus the letter count — for example: a situation that produces a large amount of something good, seven letters. Exchange your finished clues with a classmate or your AI tutor to solve, then check any disputed answers against the unit word list.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 5: The Ethics Challenge
activities.instructionsAndItems: Read these three scenarios and decide whether each advertising practice is ethical or unethical, writing two to three sentences per verdict and using unit vocabulary in your reasoning. Scenario one: a fast-food company shows happy, healthy-looking children enjoying meals that actually contain very high levels of sugar and fat. Scenario two: a mobile phone company claims its new phone has the longest battery life of any phone on sale, and independent testing backs the claim up. Scenario three: a social media influencer praises a skin cream, saying it changed her life, but never tells viewers that the company paid her to say it.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 6: Vocabulary Reinforcement Workout
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Complete three short challenges in your notebook. First, fill each blank with the best word from this box: impede, bonanza, lucrative, cunning, diminish, obsolete, momentum, apprehensive, belligerent, capacious. 1) The sale was a real ______, with everything half price. 2) His ______ plan involved spreading false rumours about a competitor. 3) The road closure will ______ traffic for several days. 4) She felt ______ about presenting to the whole school. 5) The ______ tone of his voice made everyone uncomfortable. 6) Printed encyclopaedias have become ______. 7) The business proved very ______ in its first month. 8) Once the campaign gained ______, donations poured in. 9) Cutting the budget would ______ the product's quality. 10) The ______ warehouse could store thousands of boxes. Second, match each of gusto, adversary, intricate, attentive and bountiful to its closest synonym from this scrambled list: opponent, plentiful, enthusiasm, watchful, complicated. Third, write one sentence connecting each of these words to advertising: elusive, dub, concession, emerge, indifferent.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

quizzes.question: What does 'aptitude' mean?
quizzes.options: The way a person behaves or shows their feelings. | A natural ability to do something well. | Enjoyment or enthusiasm in doing something. | Something that is given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A natural ability to do something well.
quizzes.explanation: Aptitude is a natural talent, as in the story where Imani is known for her sharp aptitude in algorithms; the other options define demeanor, gusto and concession.

quizzes.question: What does 'concession' mean?
quizzes.options: Something that is given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement. | The force or speed of something moving, especially when it is getting faster. | A person or group that opposes or fights against another. | An agreement or harmony between people or groups.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Something that is given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement.
quizzes.explanation: A concession is something surrendered to reach a deal, like Nadir's offer to collaborate next year; the other options define momentum, adversary and accord.

quizzes.question: What does 'obsolete' mean?
quizzes.options: Difficult to find, catch, or achieve. | Having a lot of space; able to hold a lot of things. | No longer used or needed because something newer exists. | Paying close attention to something or someone.
quizzes.correctAnswer: No longer used or needed because something newer exists.
quizzes.explanation: Obsolete describes things replaced by newer inventions, such as the fax machines discussed in the Before and After activity; the other options define elusive, capacious and attentive.

quizzes.question: What does 'gusto' mean?
quizzes.options: Worried or anxious about something that might happen. | Angry and ready to fight or argue. | Small and delicate in a way that is attractive. | Enjoyment or enthusiasm in doing something.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Enjoyment or enthusiasm in doing something.
quizzes.explanation: Gusto is wholehearted enthusiasm, like the energy Team Spark brought to rebuilding their drone; the other options define apprehensive, belligerent and dainty.

teacherNotes.note: Model disciplinary language aloud, teach annotation and source checking explicitly, use mixed-response modes, and give specific feedback on evidence, cohesion, viewpoint and vocabulary precision while increasing learner independence.

Encourage learners to use the AI tutor to rehearse the eight grammar focuses (prepositions preceding nouns, passive voice, participle clauses, reflexive pronouns, the second conditional, comparatives with the more and the less, compound adjectives and reported speech), to plan and check the three writing projects, to role-play the interview with Zara, and to replay the Advertising Pitch Challenge. Remind families that a parent or caregiver should stay nearby whenever a child is working online.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: There is no single correct advert to choose; award full marks when the learner identifies product, audience and at least one technique accurately, quotes or describes real wording from the advert as evidence, and gives a reasoned effectiveness rating rather than a bare number.

Accept any genuinely outdated technology; mark the three required structures rather than the choice of product — a correct passive such as fax machines were used to send documents instantly, a balanced comparative such as the more email spread, the less offices needed faxes, and a plausible second conditional about its return.

Look for a hyphenated compound adjective in the business name, a slogan under ten words, a logo description that could actually be drawn, a clearly defined audience, and an advertising paragraph containing three unit words, one passive sentence and one prepositional phrase; each missing ingredient costs one mark.

Clues must be solvable from the unit word list: the definition or gapped sentence must match the word's taught meaning and the letter count must be correct — the seven-letter example clue resolves to bonanza. Reject any clue that fits two unit words equally well.

Expected verdicts: scenario one is unethical because the healthy imagery misleads viewers about sugary meals; scenario two is ethical because the battery claim is supported by independent testing; scenario three is unethical because the paid endorsement is hidden. Award credit for reasoning and vocabulary, not just the verdict.

Sentence completion answers in order: bonanza, cunning, impede, apprehensive, belligerent, obsolete, lucrative, momentum, diminish, capacious. Synonym matches: gusto with enthusiasm, adversary with opponent, intricate with complicated, attentive with watchful, bountiful with plentiful. For the final challenge, accept any accurate advertising sentence for elusive, dub, concession, emerge and indifferent.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Correct answer: A natural ability to do something well. Aptitude names a built-in talent, as in Imani's sharp aptitude in algorithms; the distractors define demeanor, gusto and concession.

Correct answer: Something that is given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement. Nadir's collaboration offer in the story is exactly such a concession; the distractors define momentum, adversary and accord.
Correct answer: No longer used or needed because something newer exists. Obsolete fits replaced technologies such as fax machines; the distractors define elusive, capacious and attentive.
Correct answer: Enjoyment or enthusiasm in doing something. Gusto is the energy Team Spark brought to the rebuild; the distractors define apprehensive, belligerent and dainty.

Correct answer: adversary. The story names Team Horizon as Team Spark's biggest adversary; the agreement words accord and concession cannot describe a rival, and apprehensive is an adjective of worry.
Correct answer: cunning. The Beacon was created by a cunning team — clever in a deceptive way, echoed later by the copying rumours; the other adjectives describe aggression, size and plenty.
Correct answer: momentum. After the failed demo Imani felt the momentum diminish; demeanor, bonanza and concession do not describe forward force that can drain away.
Correct answer: insolent. Nadir's taunt about panicking is rude and disrespectful, so Imani refuses his insolent games; attentive, intricate and indifferent carry no rudeness.
Correct answer: capacious. The lab suddenly feels roomy and full of promise, so capacious fits; desolate would reverse the mood, and apprehensive and pungent describe feelings and smells.

Correct answer: bonanza. Social proof builds a cycle that turns an ordinary product into a bonanza of sales — a flood of something good; momentum, concession and aptitude do not name an abundant outcome.
